summary:
Last Seen on Mars is an interactive 3D story about eight machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 laser reflector, Apollo 17's rover, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity and Voyager 1. Most have gone silent; two still answer.

Visitors spin a real-textured Mars, Moon and Earth, land on each machine's true coordinates, and "talk" to it. Every machine speaks in first person, but every fact it says comes from NASA mission pages, and each one plays a real NASA recording and shows its resting place photographed from orbit by HiRISE or LROC.

Three hands-on tools turn the stories into science: a dust storm slider that recreates how Opportunity's power fell from 645 Wh to 22 Wh in 2018, a planned-vs-lived timeline (Opportunity was built for 90 days and lasted 14 years), and a signal lab that computes today's real Earth–Mars distance and light delay, and shows Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026.

It's built for school-age space fans: to make them care about the hardware first, then learn the science it made possible.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Last Seen on Mars is a scroll-driven web documentary. A real-time 3D scene (Mars, the Moon, Earth and a detailed Voyager 1 model) follows the reader through eight chapters, one per machine. Each chapter flies the camera to the machine's real landing coordinates, rotates the planet into sunlight, and opens a card with the NASA photo, key dates, stats, a live local Mars time for that site, a real NASA recording, and an orbital photo of where it rests today. Readers can open a chat and ask the machine about its mission. Its answers are written in first person, but grounded only in NASA facts.

INTERACTIVE SCIENCE

- Why they went quiet: a dust-opacity (tau) slider recreates the 2018 planet-encircling dust storm. As tau rises, the sky in the 3D scene darkens and Opportunity's solar power drops from about 645 Wh to about 22 Wh, below the ~120 Wh it needed to survive.

- Planned vs. actually lived: compares each mission's design life with how long it really worked (Spirit 90 sols vs 6 years, Opportunity 90 sols vs 14 years, Ingenuity 5 flights vs 72).

- Send a signal: uses JPL Keplerian orbital elements to compute today's real Earth–Mars distance in the browser, then shows the one-way light time and reply time for the Moon, Mars and Voyager 1. It counts down to Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth on 18 Nov 2026.

- A Mission Control certificate is unlocked after visiting all eight machines.

IMPACT

The challenge asks to introduce school-age space enthusiasts to abandoned hardware and the science behind it. We used emotion as the hook (each machine has a voice and a "last seen" moment) and real data as the payoff, so curiosity leads straight into orbital mechanics, solar power and radio communication. It runs in any browser, with no install or login.

KEEPING IT TRUE

The machines' feelings are imagined; every number, date and quote is from NASA sources and credited on the page. Images and sounds link back to their NASA source.

TOOLS

JavaScript (Vite), Three.js (WebGL, custom shaders, bloom post-processing), Lenis smooth scroll, Web Audio API, Fontsource fonts. Deployed on Vercel; code on GitHub: https://github.com/sharanyashetty013-droid/last-seen-on-mars

USE OF AI

Claude (Anthropic) was used to help write and debug code and to draft text. All photos, sounds and data are real NASA material, not AI-generated.
